expected_evidence: Ice-core geochemical anomalies (nitrate, ammonium, beryllium-10, chlorine-36 spikes) in Greenland/Arctic cores dated to ~12,900–11,700 cal BP that would indicate elevated atmospheric ionization consistent with a gamma-ray/cosmic-ray event

Deep-sea and Arctic Ocean sediment cores showing a meltwater discharge signal (oxygen-isotope excursion, freshwater lens, IRD layers) temporally coincident with the proposed ionization spike, i.e. Meltwater Pulse 1A-adjacent freshening of the Arctic/North Atlantic
Radiocarbon (14C) production anomalies in tree-ring or varve records that could be attributed to a cosmic-ray/gamma-ray ionization pulse rather than solar variability

Astronomical/astrophysical evidence for a nearby transient source (supernova remnant, gamma-ray burst progenitor) with an age consistent with ~13,000–12,000 BP, or independent modeling showing ozone depletion/NOx production matching ice-core nitrate spikes
Correlated paleoclimate proxies (pollen, glacial moraine chronology, speleothem records) showing abrupt Younger Dryas onset cooling synchronous with the proposed corroborating signal
Faunal/genetic evidence of megafaunal population disruption or extinction pulses dated to the same narrow window, sometimes cited in adjacent (and contested) Younger Dryas impact literature
response.rationale: The interval [-13000,-12001] sits right at the Younger Dryas onset, a period with unusually good preservation for geological/astronomical proxies (ice cores, varves, sediment cores) despite otherwise poor material/textual/genetic visibility this far back — geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) detectability are the highest categories available for this era, while material (0.35) and genetic (0.3) evidence are much weaker. The Younger Dryas is among the most intensively studied abrupt climate transitions, with continuous, well-dated Greenland ice cores and Arctic/North Atlantic sediment records spanning exactly this window, so the *kind* of evidence needed (isotopic/geochemical anomalies, meltwater freshening signals) could plausibly have survived and indeed has been actively searched for. However, the specific causal linkage proposed here — a meltwater pulse being 'corroborated' via a gamma-ray-ionization mechanism — combines two largely independent and non-standard causal frameworks (oceanographic freshwater forcing vs. an astrophysical ionization/GRB trigger for nitrate spikes, a fringe idea explored in real literature such as Melott & Thomas and largely inconclusive/rejected on reanalysis). This mechanistic combination is not itself a well-supported synthesis in mainstream paleoclimatology and should be flagged as `model-prior`-level speculation on my part, not an established finding from the evidence text provided. Given that (a) the relevant proxy records demonstrably survive and are queried by real science, but (b) the specific gamma-ray-ionization corroboration signal has been sought and found ambiguous/unconfirmed in the literature, an absence of strong corroborating evidence here is better explained by the hypothesis being empirically weak or unsupported than by poor preservation or low detectability. I set the composite detectability adjustment at 0.5, averaging the plausible relevant evidence channels (geological, astronomical, material, genetic) for the younger-dryas period, which is moderate-to-good — meaning a genuine absence of corroborating gamma-ray-ionization signatures in the existing ice-core/sediment record is a meaningful evidentiary gap rather than one easily excused by non-survival.
